title: A taste of next week
hookLine: the Shabbat afternoon reading begins next week's portion
carry: you start next week before this week ends

lines: A FEW SECONDS OF NEXT WEEK.
cards: TV shows end an episode with a few seconds of next week's story. Just enough so you come back. Shabbat afternoon has its own version.

The morning's long reading is done, lunch has been eaten, maybe a nap was taken. Then, late in the day, at the afternoon service, the scroll comes out of the ark again. But it isn't rolled back to this week's portion.
It's rolled forward. Three people are called up, and the congregation hears the opening of next week's portion. A preview.

teach.b: Where does this come from? The Talmud, in tractate Bava Kamma, lists ten enactments it credits to Ezra the scribe, and reading the Torah at Shabbat afternoon prayer is one of them.
The reason it gives is practical: for the shopkeepers.
As the commentator Rashi explains, these were people too busy all week to hear Torah on Monday and Thursday. Wait, Monday and Thursday? Yes.
That same short section, the opening of the coming week's portion, is read again on Monday and Thursday mornings. So the week has a rhythm. Saturday afternoon, a taste.
Monday, again. Thursday, again. And then, next Saturday morning, the whole portion.
The Talmud traces the Monday and Thursday readings to a verse from Exodus.

Right after crossing the sea, the people "went three days in the wilderness, and found no water," and when they finally found some, it was bitter. The rabbis read water as Torah. Three days without it is too long.
So the Torah is never more than three days away. In many communities, the afternoon service says a verse about timing just before the scroll comes out.
In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 69: "But as for me, let my prayer be unto Thee, O LORD, in an acceptable time." Late Shabbat afternoon is treated as one of those times. Notice what that does.
Shabbat is about stopping, but it also leans forward. Even on the day of rest, you're handed a little of what's coming.
You start next week before this week ends.

how: At Shabbat Mincha the Torah is taken out and three people are called up for the opening section of the next week's portion; the same section is read on Monday and Thursday mornings, before the full portion is read the following Shabbat.

games.q: it's Shabbat afternoon, and the Torah comes out again. which portion do they read from?
o: the opening of next week's portion.
games.why: the opening of the coming week's portion: a taste, repeated Monday and Thursday.

practice: If you can, find the name of next week's portion and read its first few verses. If not, picture the week ahead, not as a list of tasks but as a story about to begin, and let yourself taste the one thing you're looking forward to.

wordCard.voice: Ezra, the scribe credited with the custom of reading a taste of the coming week's Torah portion on Shabbat afternoon, and again Monday and Thursday.
